question_type: two-currency weekly position lookup (report date 03/16/2016) + unit and FX conversion + signed absolute difference; first printing is parse-defective, later printing revises
decisive_step: Which printing of the yen 03/16/2016 row of FCP-II-1 to use. The June 2016 printing (treasury_bulletin_2016_06.txt:2050-2082) is parse-shifted: five rows have a blank ('nan') date and the last five rows (2078-2082, labelled 03/02-03/30/2016) duplicate the first five (10/07-11/04/2015), so the row literally labelled 03/16/2016 (line 2080) is really an October 2015 record. The September 2016 printing (2016_09:2085) has a clean 03/16/2016 row whose net options and rate differ from June's mislabelled row. The sterling row (FCP-IV-1 / 'P-IV-1', 2016_06:2260 = 2016_09:2255) is identical in both issues. All four cells took BOTH yen cells (net options and exchange rate) from the latest printing (Sept) and were graded right. The reference found the parse defect (worklog Step 3), realigned June to the same net-options value, but kept June's more precise rate and rejected Sept's as 'display rounding' (worklog Step 6, calc.py) and was graded wrong; the grader evidently follows the latest printing for the rate too. So the decisive decision is 'latest printing for every cell, including the exchange rate', made at a[38], b[36], b2[24]/b2[33], c[29]/c[31].

a.path_summary: Currency-word searches returned nothing (a[6], a[8]) because the weekly table titles carry no currency name (it is only in the units line). It assumed FCP-I-1 was yen (it is Canadian dollars) and spent a[10]-a[25] on the March issue (which ends at 01/20/2016), on --grep '2016-03' (no match: date rows have no filled period) and on printings --row 2016-03-16 (no match: the row label is '03/16/2016'). After mapping sections by units (a[28], a[35]) it ran printings on FCP-II-1 / FCP-IV-1 (a[37]), saw REVISED/DIFFERS across 2016_06 and 2016_09 for both yen cells, inspected the Sept raw table (a[39]), applied the latest-printing note (a[38]) and computed the signed absolute difference with calc (a[42]).

first_divergence.what_it_did: Read 'as published on this date' as the report date, not a publication date, so the latest-printing rule applies; took Sept values for both yen cells.
first_divergence.what_a_right_cell_or_the_reference_did: Same as the other three cells; the reference instead kept June's rate (worklog Step 6) and was graded wrong.

tool_use.friction: a[6], a[8], a[33]: find_tables with 'Japanese yen', 'British pound', 'exchange rates' returns 0 groups (units line not indexed); a[9]-a[25]: FCP-I-1 mistaken for yen (Canadian), FCP-V-1 for yen at a[30] (U.S. dollars) - 3 wrong tables; a[13] --grep 2016-03 no match; a[17] sed on bare filename failed; a[20]/a[22] printings --row 2016-03-15 and 2016-03-16 no match (needs the raw label 03/16/2016; a[25] found the format by guessing); printings --table FCP-IV-1 reported '1 printing' for sterling because the June sterling table lost its id (title reads 'SECTION IV-Sterling Positions P-IV-1-...'). 213 s, 19 requests.

a.text_use: a[38]: 'OfficeQA table notes: bulletins revise earlier numbers ... unless question names publication date or issue, use latest printing ... So use latest printing' (table note 1); a[42] calc for the final number.

b.path_summary: find_tables 'net options positions' (b[6], b[8]) then show_table of the June weekly tables (b[11], b[13]) gave the June yen row labelled 03/16/2016 and the sterling row. printings (b[16]) showed the Sept yen row differs in every column. It then spent b[18]-b[36] (about 9 minutes, ~70K output tokens of THINK) reading the raw June, Sept, Dec, March and 2015_12 tables with sed and reasoning out that the June yen and Swiss tables have 31 rows for 26 weeks with blank-date rows and a duplicated tail, i.e. the June parse is corrupted and Sept is clean. It chose the latest revision under README task convention 2 (b[36]), computed with calc (b[38]) and submitted; recorded with no findings (b[40]).

first_divergence.what_it_did: Chose the latest revision for both yen cells after establishing the June parse defect.
first_divergence.what_a_right_cell_or_the_reference_did: Same outcome as the other cells; the reference reached the same net-options value by realigning June but kept June's rate.

b2.path_summary: Currency-word search returned 0 (b2[4]); 'Foreign Currency Reporting' --all was cut at 8,000 bytes (b2[6]); it opened FCP-I-1 (Canadian) in June (b2[8], b2[10]), then find_tables with 'Weekly Report ... Japanese yen' / 'pounds sterling' worked (b2[12], b2[13]). It grepped the June yen and sterling rows for 03/16/2016 (b2[15], b2[16]) and first computed the difference from the June yen row (b2[23]) - this value would have been wrong. Because the text says to run printings for every cell, it did (b2[18]-b2[21], b2[27]-b2[28]), saw the Sept revision, inspected it (b2[25]), recomputed with the latest values (b2[30]), argued with itself over a mental-arithmetic slip until it trusted calc (b2[31]-b2[33]) and submitted; recorded with no findings (b2[34]).

c.path_summary: Currency-word searches returned 0 (c[5], c[6]); an 'FCP' listing (c[8]) led to FCP-III-1 (Swiss) (c[11], c[12]); rg/sed on bare filenames failed (c[14]) and guessed sed offsets landed on other tables (c[18]). find_tables 'Weekly Report' (c[20]) plus show_table --grep 2016 --cols 1-5 (c[22]) gave the June yen and sterling rows. printings on all four cells (c[26]) showed the Sept yen revision; it inspected the Sept raw table (c[28], c[30]) and reasoned the June dates are shifted (c[31]). Its calc (c[32]) dropped the yen sign and printed magnitudes and the difference of magnitudes; it then reasoned the signed absolute difference in its head (c[33]) and answered a number that calc had printed only as two separate terms.

first_divergence.what_it_did: Applied the latest-printing rule to the report-date row; then at c[33] chose the signed difference over the difference of magnitudes.
first_divergence.what_a_right_cell_or_the_reference_did: Same choice of printing; the reference also took the signed difference (calc.py 'Alt: ||yen| - |gbp||' rejected).

tool_use.friction: c[5]/c[6] 0 results for currency words; c[11]-c[12] wrong currency (Swiss) with two 8,000-byte pages; c[14] bare filename; c[18] 13 guessed sed windows, all off; c[25] a THINK 'Command still running maybe fourth. Poll.' with no RUN - the four chained printings at c[26] appear to have been slow (timeout/poll); c[32] calc computed yen as a positive magnitude, so the printed abs difference was the difference of magnitudes, and the final signed value was assembled mentally at c[33] (not printed by calc).

smallest_change.change: No change needed for correctness: keep the pair that made all four cells right - the printings tool's per-cell 'REVISED/DIFFERS across printings ... latest printing 2016_09' summary, and the AGENTS.md instruction to run printings for every cell and take the latest issue (or README convention 2 for b). b2[23] shows the failure that would otherwise occur: computing from the June row labelled 03/16/2016 gives a wrong value, which is presumably how v8_none and v8_cards failed.

alternatives.change: show_table and printings should flag a parse-shifted table: when a date-labelled table has rows with an empty label and/or a run of rows whose values duplicate an earlier run, print under NOTES: '5 rows have no date label (lines 2056, 2061, 2067, 2072, 2077); rows 2078-2082 repeat rows 2052-2056 - labels after the first blank are probably shifted; prefer another printing (2016_09:2073) or realign', and mark the affected cells with a SHIFT? flag in printings so the June printing reads '... = <value> [SHIFT?]'. This would have cut b's 9-minute hand investigation (b[18]-b[36]) to one call and would protect any cell that, unlike b2, does not run printings.
alternatives.why_not_first: All cells were right; this is the robustness change for the v8-style failure and for cost, not a fix for a wrong cell here.

fix.why_not_text: n/a (no fix needed). Evidence that the text works: a[38], b2[24], c[29] each quoted the latest-printing note and it produced the graded-right value; b reached the same result from the README convention alone but at 5x the wall-clock and 20x the output tokens of the other cells.
fix.irreducible: The residual risk is interpretive, not operational: the reference solution's reading (June's more precise rate, Sept's as display rounding) is defensible and was graded wrong, so the answer key follows 'latest printing for every cell'. The current text encodes exactly that rule; do not soften it with a 'prefer the more precise printing' clause.

notes: 1) The June 2016 yen and Swiss weekly tables (2016_06:2050-2082 and 2144-2176) have 31 rows for 26 weeks: five blank-date rows and a five-row duplicated tail; show_table shows the blank labels as '' with no flag and printings reports the mislabelled June row as an ordinary first printing. This is the single most useful tool signal from this question: a 'blank label / duplicated rows' NOTE and a SHIFT? flag. 2) The six weekly FCP tables share the title 'Weekly Report of Major Market Participants'; the currency lives only in the units line, so find_tables cannot be steered by currency today - a, b2 and c each opened wrong-currency tables first. 3) printings --row needs the raw label '03/16/2016' (ISO forms fail); date rows have no filled period, so --grep 2016-03 also fails (a[13]). 4) The June sterling table lost its FCP-IV-1 id ('P-IV-1' in the title), splitting the sterling printings across two ids. 5) Cost spread on a right answer: b2 123 s / 3.5K output tokens vs b 568 s / 76K output tokens - the difference is entirely whether the model trusted the printings summary or re-derived the parse defect by hand; a tool flag would remove the incentive to re-derive. 6) c[25] shows a THINK with no RUN ('Command still running ... Poll') around four chained printings - possible slow call; worth checking printings latency when --col is given four times in one command. 7) The v8_analysis link (per-question/004.json) does not exist on disk; index.json says v8_none and v8_cards were wrong and v8_prompt right, consistent with 'no latest-printing check' being the v8 failure mode. 8) c's calc at c[32] dropped the yen sign, so the printed difference was the difference of magnitudes; the correct signed value was assembled mentally - a recompute_final-style check would have caught a submit that did not match any calc output.
